clue.text: Damn inspiring old programme

indicators.note: inspiring means breathing in, so one word takes another inside itself

parts.note: to damn is to curse
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Someone swearing at an old television programme they are watching again.
explanation.walkthrough: The curse breathes in the old letter after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A course is a planned programme of study or treatment, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Bright guards are making knife

indicators.note: something that guards stands around what it protects, enclosing it

parts.note: bright means intelligent
an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated a

explanation.surface: A clever person protects the people who make knives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are' is not the verb but the metric unit of area, a hundred square metres.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleaver is a heavy broad-bladed knife used by butchers to chop meat.

clue.text: American specified female attendant

parts.note: US abbreviates the United States
her is the pronoun pointing to a particular woman

explanation.surface: A US woman chosen to be a helper at an event.
explanation.definitionFit: An usher is a person who shows guests to their seats, an attendant at a wedding, theatre or court.

clue.text: Nazis drinking house wines as affectation

indicators.note: someone drinking takes a liquid inside, so the outer word swallows the others

parts.note: the SS was the Nazi paramilitary organisation
HO is the standard abbreviation for house
taken as written

explanation.surface: Nazis knocking back the house wine as a pretentious pose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'house wines' reads as one phrase, but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Showiness is ostentatious display meant to impress, a form of affectation.

clue.text: When to cut green targets for idiot

indicators.note: a word that cuts into another is set inside it, splitting it

parts.note: in lawn bowls, played on a green, the small white target ball is the jack
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: Someone asks when to trim the targets on a golf green, for a fool's benefit.
explanation.walkthrough: The bowling green's targets are jacks; AS cuts in before the final S.
explanation.definitionFit: A jackass, literally a male donkey, is slang for a stupid person or idiot.

clue.text: Japanese seat of learning exercises right to display tree

parts.note: J abbreviates Japanese
uni is short for university
PE is physical education, school exercises
R abbreviates right

explanation.surface: A Japanese university's exercise programme properly shows off a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The juniper is an evergreen coniferous tree or shrub whose berries flavour gin.

clue.text: King meeting maniac regularly for fun

parts.note: CR stands for Carolus Rex, King Charles

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A king meets a madman routinely, for amusement.
explanation.walkthrough: CR, Carolus Rex, is the Latin cipher of a King Charles.
explanation.definitionFit: Craic is an Irish word for fun, enjoyable conversation and good times.

clue.text: Judge slightly occupied by Republican charge

indicators.note: a place occupied by someone has them inside it

parts.note: a bit means slightly
R abbreviates Republican
a rate is a fee or charge

explanation.surface: A judge somewhat taken over by a Republican accusation.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes in after the first letter of A BIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To arbitrate is to judge a dispute as an impartial third party.

clue.text: She stores art in French department

indicators.note: a thing that stores another keeps it inside

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman keeps her artworks in a department in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'department' could be a shop's; here it is a French administrative region.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sarthe is a department of western France, home of Le Mans, named after its river.

clue.text: Alert as comedian struck

parts.note: a wit is a funny person
hit is past tense of the verb, meaning struck

explanation.surface: Someone is wide awake because a comic was attacked.
explanation.definitionFit: With it is an informal phrase for mentally sharp and aware, so alert.

clue.text: African is playing the piano around 1

indicators.note: around means the reworked letters go on either side of the other piece
playing suggests the words are being performed freely, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: letters to be rearranged
the numeral one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: An African musician is playing the piano at about one o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: '1' looks like a cross-reference to 1-across, but it is just the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: An Ethiopian is a person from Ethiopia, a country in the Horn of Africa, so is African.

clue.text: Cautionary signal — slope's beginning to be ignored

indicators.note: the start of the word is to be ignored, so its first letter is dropped

parts.note: camber is the slight slope across a road surface

explanation.surface: A road sign warns that the slope's start is not to be ignored.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the first letter of CAMBER.
explanation.definitionFit: The amber traffic light warns drivers that the signal is about to change, so it is a cautionary signal.

clue.text: Composer exaggerated when naked

indicators.note: naked means stripped of covering, so the word loses its outer letters

parts.note: to overdo something is to exaggerate it

explanation.surface: A critic complains that a composer overplayed things when performing nude.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip the first and last letters from OVERDID to leave Giuseppe Verdi.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi was the nineteenth-century Italian composer of operas such as Aida and La Traviata.

clue.text: Spring put an end to kid's game

parts.note: to spring is to hop
to scotch a rumour or plan is to put an end to it

explanation.surface: An instruction to leap and halt a child's play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' reads like the season, but it is the verb meaning jump.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopscotch is a children's playground game of hopping through squares chalked on the ground.

clue.text: Call otolaryngology department, having gaping lips

parts.note: to call someone on the phone is to ring them
ENT, ear nose and throat, is the hospital department for otolaryngology

explanation.surface: A patient with open-mouthed lips is told to phone the ear, nose and throat clinic.
explanation.walkthrough: A rare word: botanists use it for flowers, such as snapdragons, with two gaping lips.
explanation.definitionFit: Ringent is a technical adjective, from Latin for opening the mouth wide, describing a corolla with widely parted lips.

clue.text: In game of cards Jack drops, followed by Queen, to give easy decision

parts.note: in cribbage, 'his nob' is the jack of the turned-up suit
rain falls as drops
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the cipher of Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: In a card game, the jack is discarded and then a queen played, an obvious move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack drops' reads like a card being played; drops is its own piece meaning rain. Cribbage is a card game scored on a pegboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-brainer is informal for a choice so obvious it needs no thought.

clue.text: Oddly, Raid insect repellent is something the chippy uses

indicators.note: oddly means take the letters in the odd-numbered positions of the next word

parts.note: first and third letters of the word

indicators.note: repellent read as repelled, driven back, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: a wasp is a stinging insect

explanation.surface: A carpenter uses Raid insect spray, strangely, as a tool.
explanation.walkthrough: Raid is a brand of insect spray, which is what makes 'insect repellent' a convincing phrase. A chippy is British slang for a carpenter.
explanation.definitionFit: A ripsaw is a handsaw for cutting wood along the grain, a standard tool of a carpenter.

clue.text: Writing with Sexy Sue

parts.note: prose is ordinary written language
cute can mean sexually attractive

explanation.surface: Writing a story about a glamorous woman named Sue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sue' looks like a woman's name, but it is the verb meaning take to court.
explanation.definitionFit: To sue someone is to take legal action against them, which is to prosecute in a broad sense.

clue.text: Slags off advanced coaches

parts.note: A is a standard abbreviation for advanced
coaches are long-distance buses

explanation.surface: Someone runs down the latest, more advanced sports coaches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coaches' reads as trainers but means vehicles. To slag off is British slang for criticising harshly.
explanation.definitionFit: To abuse someone is to insult them, which is what slagging off means in British slang.

clue.text: Pick a fight with celebrity running around Thailand

indicators.note: around means the outer pair of words surround the abbreviation

parts.note: a celebrity is a star
T is the international vehicle code for Thailand
a machine that is on is running

explanation.surface: A famous person jogging in Thailand provokes a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running around' reads as one phrase, but running is its own piece; T is the international car code for Thailand.
explanation.definitionFit: To start on someone is an idiom meaning to begin attacking or criticising them, picking a fight.

clue.text: European inhabitants love new clothes

indicators.note: clothes as a verb means covers, so the phrase wraps around the answer

parts.note: runs from the end of the first word into the last

explanation.surface: The people who live there adore new clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothes' looks like a noun for garments, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A Slovene is a native of Slovenia, a central European country, so is European.

clue.text: Cross left out as show of irony?

definitions.note: the question mark marks a definition by example

indicators.note: out means removed, so the named letter is taken away

parts.note: a saltire is a diagonal X-shaped cross, as on Scotland's flag
L abbreviates left

explanation.surface: An angry person excluded, as an ironic display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like the adjective angry, but it is the St Andrew's cross. Remove the L from SALTIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Satire is a genre that mocks folly, often using irony, so a satirical show displays irony.

clue.text: Gospel of electronic keyboard player and composer is ignored

indicators.note: the word is in the clue is to be ignored, so those letters are dropped from the name

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for electronic
Vangelis, the Greek synthesiser player who wrote the Chariots of Fire score

explanation.surface: A synth player and composer's gospel music being overlooked.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the final IS from Vangelis, the clue's own word 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Evangel is an archaic word for the gospel, the good news of Christ, from the Greek for good message.

clue.text: Mass producers disheartened old man

parts.note: a gram is a unit of mass

indicators.note: disheartened means losing the heart, so only the outer letters stay

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: Factory producers of goods in bulk left a pensioner downcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass producers' reads as one phrase, but splits apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Gramps is an informal word for grandfather, and old man is also slang for father or a familiar elder.

clue.text: Reportedly went on courses, primarily to get waterborne vessel driving skills

indicators.note: reportedly signals a word heard rather than read, so another spelling is wanted

parts.note: a jockey rode on racecourses

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: opening letter
a raft is a simple floating craft

explanation.surface: A rower or jockey picks up boat-handling and driving skills on various courses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'courses' does double duty: racecourses for the riding, then its own first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Roadcraft is the skill and judgment needed to drive safely on roads, the name of the police drivers' manual.

clue.text: Hunt Charles I of England

parts.note: Chas is the short form of Charles

indicators.note: I as the numeral one points to the first letter of the word after

parts.note: number one letter of the word

explanation.surface: A king's name, Charles I of England.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a historical monarch, but 'I of England' means its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To chase is to pursue or hunt, and a hunt is also called a chase.

clue.text: On return, famed epidemiologist nurses American's swelling

indicators.note: on return means the letters are read heading back the way they came
nurses means holds closely, so the words cradle the answer within them

parts.note: letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A well-known disease expert, coming back home, cares for an American patient's swelling.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition flags American spelling: British English writes oedema.
explanation.definitionFit: Edema is the US spelling of oedema, a swelling caused by fluid collecting in body tissues.

clue.text: Anger returned about Heather

indicators.note: returned means sent back the way it came, so it is read from the end

parts.note: ire is anger
ca, for circa, means about

explanation.surface: Someone's fury flared up again concerning a woman named Heather.
explanation.walkthrough: Heather reads as a woman's name; it is the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is the botanical genus of heaths and heathers, so it names the plant.

clue.text: Perhaps Ray thanks Ray?

definitions.note: the question mark flags that Ray here is the fish, not the man

parts.note: Ray is a man's name, so a Ray is an example of a man
ta is informal British for thanks

explanation.surface: One person called Ray seemingly thanking another Ray.
explanation.walkthrough: The first Ray is a man's name; the second, the definition, is the fish, which the question mark signals.
explanation.definitionFit: The manta is the largest kind of ray, a flat cartilaginous fish with wing-like fins.

clue.text: Painful nonsense about war hero

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: rot is a word for nonsense
Alan Turing, the codebreaker at Bletchley Park in the Second World War

explanation.surface: Hurtful rubbish written about a wartime hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Turing was persecuted after the war, which gives the surface its painful edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Torturing used as an adjective means agonising, causing great suffering, so it means painful.

clue.text: Advocate stops son becoming medical practitioner

indicators.note: stops in the sense of plugs, filling a gap inside the other word

parts.note: taken as written
to advocate a course is to urge it

explanation.surface: A lawyer prevents a son from training as a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advocate' looks like the lawyer, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgeon is a doctor who performs operations, a kind of medical practitioner.

clue.text: Happen to call about absolutely nothing

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: to give someone a bell is British slang for to call them
FA, for sweet Fanny Adams, is British slang for nothing at all

explanation.surface: Something happens to make a phone call about nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The bell wraps around FA.
explanation.definitionFit: To befall someone is to happen to them, usually something unwelcome.
